papers.title_in_file: Explainable AI for Trees: From Local Explanations to Global Understanding
papers.version_note: The file is the arXiv v1 preprint (1905.04610v1, 11 May 2019) titled 'Explainable AI for Trees: From Local Explanations to Global Understanding'. The record id names the later published version 'From local explanations to global understanding with explainable AI for trees'. The content matches the record.
sections_read: 2.1 Tree-based models can be more accurate than neural networks
2.2 Tree-based models can be more interpretable than linear models
2.3 Current local explanations for tree-based models are inconsistent
2.4 Model-agnostic local explanations are slow and variable
2.5 TreeExplainer provides fast local explanations with guaranteed consistency
2.6 TreeExplainer extends local explanations to measure interaction effects
2.7 Local explanations from TreeExplainer can be used as building blocks for global understanding (2.7.1 to 2.7.5)
Methods 1 to 18 (including Algorithms 1 to 3 and Theorems 1 and 2)

papers.what_it_is: A preprint presenting TreeExplainer, an exact polynomial-time algorithm (Tree SHAP) for Shapley-value explanations of tree ensembles, SHAP interaction values, and five tools that combine local explanations (summary, dependence, interaction, monitoring, embeddings), demonstrated on three medical datasets and benchmarks.

assertions.value: The paper states that only one feature attribution method based on the conditional-expectation set function satisfies the three properties of local accuracy, consistency and missingness: the classic Shapley values averaged over all feature orderings. The authors say the equivalent result was previously presented in a cited work and follows from cooperative game theory.
quotes: Only one possible feature attribution method based on fx satisﬁes Properties 1, 2 and 3:
The equivalent of Theorem 1 has been previously presented in [41]
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the result to earlier work and does not reprove it here.

assertions.value: The paper proves that for binary features, in the limit of an infinite ensemble of totally random fully developed trees, the Saabas values equal the SHAP values. The proof argues that each tree's decision path is a random feature ordering, so averaging over the ensemble reproduces the Shapley ordering average.
quotes: In the limit of an inﬁnite ensemble of totally random fully developed trees on binary features the Saabas
values equal the SHAP values [41]
Taking the average of the Saabas values over the ensemble
assertions.certainty_reason: The theorem is stated with its conditions and followed by a proof in Methods 9.
assertions.reader_inference: The proof is a short argument; it covers only the idealized infinite random-tree limit, not finite greedily built ensembles.

assertions.value: The authors state that Tree SHAP has worst-case complexity proportional to the number of trees times the number of leaves times the square of the maximum tree depth, which they call an exponential complexity improvement over previous exact Shapley methods.
quotes: Letting T be the number of trees, D the maximum depth of any tree, and L the number of leaves, Tree SHAP has worst case complexity of
This represents an exponential complexity improvement over previous exact Shapley methods
assertions.certainty_reason: The bound is stated with its variables and derived in the paper's complexity analysis (Methods 10.1.2, p.22).
assertions.reader_inference: The formula itself is printed with a line break in the text layer and is not quoted here.

assertions.value: The authors state that, assuming the weight calculation takes constant time, Independent Tree SHAP does constant work at each node, giving time proportional to the number of trees times the number of background samples times the number of leaves.
quotes: If we assume CALCWEIGHT takes constant time
Repeating this algorithm for each tree and for each background
assertions.certainty_reason: Conditions (constant-time weight lookup) and derivation are given in the complexity analysis.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experiments in the paper used 200 background samples to produce low variance estimates with Independent Tree SHAP.
quotes: Note that for the experiments in this paper we used R = 200 background samples to produce low variance estimates.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that for moderate sized models TreeExplainer is several orders of magnitude faster than model-agnostic alternatives and has zero estimation variability.
quotes: For moderate sized models, TreeExplainer is several orders of magnitude faster than model-agnostic alternatives,
and has zero estimation variability
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from the authors' own timing experiments on simulated and kidney data.

assertions.value: The authors state that the model-agnostic baselines were run with a single background reference sample and that the reported Kernel SHAP and IME times are only a lower bound, so the speed comparison uses favourable settings for those baselines.
quotes: We also only used a single background reference sample for the model-agnostic approaches.
the reported times are only a lower bound
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limitation on their own measured comparison.

assertions.value: The authors report that computing low variance model-agnostic Shapley estimates for the kidney dataset experiments would have taken almost 2 CPU days for basic explanations and over 3 CPU years for interaction values.
quotes: would have taken almost 2 CPU days for basic explanations
over 3 CPU years for interaction values
assertions.certainty_reason: Extrapolated cost estimate from the authors' convergence experiments.
assertions.reader_inference: Low variance was defined by the authors as a standard deviation below 1% of the tenth largest feature impact.

assertions.value: The authors cite prior work for the statement that computing Shapley values exactly is NP-hard in general, requiring a summation over all feature subsets.
quotes: computing them exactly is NP-hard
requiring a summation over all feature subsets
assertions.certainty_reason: Result attributed to a cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that Saabas values are inconsistent: a model can be modified to make a feature clearly more important while the Saabas value attributed to that feature decreases.
quotes: we can modify a model to make a feature clearly more important, and yet the Saabas
value attributed to that feature will decrease
they do not match the SHAP values, and so must violate consistency
assertions.certainty_reason: Shown with an explicit counterexample on small trees (Supplementary Figure 2) and an argument from the ordering average.

assertions.value: The authors state that in multi-way AND trees no feature should get more credit than another, yet Saabas values give splits near the root much less credit than splits near the leaves.
quotes: yet Saabas values give splits near the root much less credit than splits near the leaves
assertions.certainty_reason: Shown on constructed AND trees (Supplementary Figure 1A) rather than on real data.

assertions.value: The authors state that Saabas values are computed like SHAP values but consider only the single feature ordering defined by a tree's decision path rather than averaging over all orderings, and that they satisfy local accuracy.
quotes: rather than averaging over all feature orderings, Saabas values only consider the single ordering
Saabas values satisfy the local accuracy property
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the definitions of Saabas values and Shapley values given in Methods 6 and 9.

assertions.value: The paper defines local accuracy as requiring attribution values to sum up to the model output, and consistency as requiring that if a feature's contribution increases or stays the same regardless of other inputs, its attribution should not decrease.
quotes: the explanation’s attribution values should sum up to the output f (x).
Consistency states that if a model changes so that some feature’s contribution increases or stays the same regardless
of the other inputs, that input’s attribution should not decrease.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definitions the paper's guarantees depend on.

assertions.value: The authors report that TreeExplainer outperforms alternative explanation methods across a benchmark of 21 local explanation metrics that they designed, applied to eight explanation methods across three model types and three datasets.
quotes: TreeExplainer consistently outperforms alternative methods across a benchmark of 21
We designed 21 metrics to comprehensively evaluate the performance of local explanation methods
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical benchmark by the method's own authors on metrics they chose.
assertions.reader_inference: Benchmark metrics were designed by the same authors who propose the method; the main text shows only the kidney dataset results, with the other results in supplementary figures.

assertions.value: The Figure 3 caption states that, as expected, Saabas becomes a better approximation to the Shapley values, and so a better attribution method, as the number of trees increases.
quotes: Note that, as expected, Saabas becomes a better approximation to the Shapley values
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical observation across decision tree, random forest and boosted tree rows of one benchmark.

assertions.value: The Figure 3 caption states that when the experiments were repeated in two synthetic datasets, TreeExplainer remained the top performing method.
quotes: When these experiments were repeated in two synthetic datasets, TreeExplainer remained the top performing method
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from the authors' own benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors state that the user study used four simple models and 33 English-speaking individuals in the U.S. on Amazon Mechanical Turk, who allocated credit among input features for three samples per model.
quotes: we use four simple models and ask 33 english speaking individuals in the U.S. on Amazon
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that Shapley-value based explanation methods agree with the human consensus attribution in all the scenarios tested, whereas the heuristic Saabas method differs significantly from the consensus in several non-linear cases.
quotes: Shapley value based explanation methods agree with human intuition in all the scenarios we tested
the heuristic Saabas method diﬀers signiﬁcantly from the human consensus in several of the nonlinear cases
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical user study with small models and a plurality-vote consensus.
assertions.reader_inference: The consensus for some scenarios was a plurality of widely spread answers (Supplementary Figures 35 and 36).

assertions.value: The Supplementary Figure 6 caption states that, because the small human-understandable models have only three features, model-agnostic Shapley methods are accurate and comparable with TreeExplainer in the user study.
quotes: models have only three features, model agnostic Shapley methods are accurate and so comparable with
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state what the user study cannot distinguish.
assertions.reader_inference: The user study does not separate TreeExplainer from sampling-based Shapley estimators.

over 10,745 visits with the goal of using 333 features
